nameStory: The Zostera Shrimp gets its name from its favorite hangout spot - eelgrass beds, where the scientific name for eelgrass is Zostera marina. These tiny shrimps are so closely tied to eelgrass that they've essentially become the underwater equivalent of apartment dwellers, rarely venturing far from their leafy green neighborhood. The name perfectly captures this species' lifestyle as the ultimate eelgrass specialist.
description: The Zostera Shrimp is a tiny, translucent marine crustacean that rarely exceeds half an inch in length. These delicate shrimps have a distinctive humped back that gives their family its common name, along with long, thread-like antennae that can be longer than their entire body. They're masters of camouflage, often appearing nearly invisible as they cling to eelgrass blades with their slender legs. Despite their small size, they're active little creatures that can be spotted darting between grass blades when disturbed.

idTips.label: Humped back profile
idTips.description: The back curves upward in a distinctive hump behind the head, giving the shrimp a bent or arched appearance when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body is nearly see-through with a glassy, crystal-like quality that makes internal organs faintly visible, feeling delicate and soft if gently handled

idTips.label: Extra-long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thread-thin and often extend well beyond the body length, constantly moving and twitching to sense the water around them

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Adults typically measure only 0.3-0.5 inches long, about the size of a large grain of rice or small paperclip

idTips.label: Eelgrass association
idTips.description: Almost always found clinging to or moving among eelgrass blades, rarely seen in open water or other habitats

habitat: Zostera Shrimp live exclusively in shallow coastal waters where eelgrass (Zostera marina) grows, typically in protected bays, estuaries, and salt ponds. Look for them in depths of 3-15 feet where the water is calm enough for eelgrass beds to flourish. They prefer areas with good water circulation but protection from heavy wave action, often in the same spots where you'd find blue mussels, hermit crabs, and small fish taking shelter among the grass.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as water temperatures rise, and this is when they're easiest to spot as they begin feeding more actively on tiny organisms in the eelgrass.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when populations are highest and most visible. Look for them during calm, sunny days when the water is clearest.
seasonality.fall: Still present and active in early fall, but may be harder to find as eelgrass begins to die back and water temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and very difficult to observe, though some adults may survive in deeper, more protected parts of eelgrass beds.

funFact: Zostera Shrimp can change their body color slightly to match different shades of eelgrass, and when threatened, they can snap their tail so forcefully that they rocket backward through the water like tiny underwater jet engines!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, translucent shrimp species in eelgrass beds, but the distinctive humped back profile sets Zostera Shrimp apart from the more straight-backed grass shrimp (Palaemonetes species). Remember: 'Humped like a tiny underwater camel' for Zostera Shrimp versus the straighter profile of grass shrimp.
compareHints: Since this is the only Hippolyte species commonly found in New England eelgrass beds, compare it with the more common grass shrimp (Palaemonetes species) which have straighter backs and tend to be slightly larger. Zostera Shrimp also have proportionally longer antennae and a more delicate, glassy appearance compared to the sturdier-looking grass shrimp.
